project.name: mike
project.description: Legal document assistant with a Next.js frontend and an Express backend, using Supabase Auth/Postgres, Cloudflare R2-compatible object storage, and Anthropic/Gemini/OpenAI model providers for document drafting, review, and processing. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what Mike is: a legal document assistant built from a Next.js frontend and an Express backend, with Supabase providing auth and Postgres, an R2/S3-compatible bucket holding document files, and at least one LLM provider key (Anthropic, Gemini, or OpenAI) powering the assistant. It also explains the repo layout and the database convention you will see later: schema.sql for fresh databases, incremental migrations for existing ones. Keep this two-app shape in mind — the rest of the tour walks the backend first, then the frontend that consumes it.

tour.title: Backend Entry Point
tour.description: The Express server entry point is the map of the whole API: it configures helmet, CORS, JSON body limits, and tiered rate limiters, then mounts eight feature routers — chat, projects, project chat, documents, tabular reviews, workflows, user, and downloads. Each router corresponds to a feature you will meet again on the frontend side of the tour. Everything the UI does ultimately arrives here as an HTTP request.

tour.title: The API Route Map
tour.description: These five routers, all mounted in Step 2, define Mike's feature surface. The chat router runs the streaming LLM conversation loop with credit enforcement; the documents router handles upload, DOCX-to-PDF conversion, versioning, and tracked-change accept/reject; the projects router manages legal matters with folders, sharing, and batch uploads; the tabular router does spreadsheet-style extraction across many documents at once; and the workflows router stores reusable, shareable prompt templates. Notice the pattern: routes stay thin and delegate real work to the lib/ modules we visit next.

tour.title: Authentication and Access Control
tour.description: Every router from Step 3 sits behind this security layer. The auth middleware validates the Supabase bearer token and attaches userId and userEmail to the request, the supabase module provides the service-role client that routes use to reach Postgres, and access.ts enforces ownership and email-based sharing rules for projects, documents, and tabular reviews. These are among the most depended-upon files in the backend — nearly every data access flows through them.

tour.title: Document Storage and Processing
tour.description: This is the legal-document heart of the backend, serving the documents and projects routes from Step 3. Uploads pass through the multer middleware, get converted from DOCX to PDF via LibreOffice when needed, and land in Cloudflare R2 object storage under deterministic keys; documentVersions tracks each immutable version. The standout is docxTrackedChanges: a pure-TypeScript OOXML engine that parses word/document.xml and applies or resolves Word tracked changes — the feature that lets the assistant edit legal documents like a colleague using Track Changes.
tour.languageLesson: A .docx file is just a ZIP archive of XML files (the OOXML format). The main body lives in word/document.xml, and Word's tracked changes are ordinary <w:ins> and <w:del> elements inside it — which is why a pure-TypeScript library can read and rewrite them without Microsoft Word.

tour.title: Multi-Provider LLM Adapters
tour.description: Mike supports Anthropic, Gemini, and OpenAI through a classic adapter pattern. The provider-neutral contracts in types.ts define one shape for messages, tool definitions, and streaming callbacks; each provider adapter translates that shape into its native SDK or API and drives a multi-turn tool-use loop; and index.ts is the router facade that picks the adapter from the model id. This is why the rest of the codebase never mentions a specific provider — it only speaks the shared contract.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript's structural typing makes adapter patterns cheap: each provider module just exports functions matching the shared stream-parameter and callback types from types.ts, and the facade can dispatch to any of them without classes or inheritance.

tour.title: The Agentic Chat Engine
tour.description: chatTools.ts is the brain that the chat and project-chat routes from Step 3 invoke: it defines the system prompt and the tool schemas (read, find, generate, and edit documents, plus project, tabular, and workflow extras), builds the document context, executes each tool call, and orchestrates the streaming loop through the LLM layer from Step 6. Its companion tools.ts converts those provider-neutral tool definitions into the native Claude and Gemini schemas. Together they turn a plain chat endpoint into an agent that can actually read and edit the documents stored in Step 5.

tour.title: The Database Schema
tour.description: The consolidated Supabase Postgres schema defines the 16 tables that everything so far reads and writes. projects model a legal matter with a client-matter number and a shared_with collaborator list (the sharing rules Step 4 enforces); documents and document_versions mirror the storage versioning from Step 5, with version rows pointing at the original file and converted PDF in R2; and chats persist the conversations the engine in Step 7 produces. The schema also installs an auth signup trigger and indexes, making it the single source of truth for a fresh deployment.
tour.languageLesson: This repo uses a common two-track SQL convention: schema.sql is the full snapshot you run once on a fresh database, while backend/migrations/ holds incremental, ordered changes for databases that already have data. Never run the full snapshot over production — apply migrations instead.

tour.title: Frontend App Shell
tour.description: Switching to the Next.js side: the root layout loads the Inter and EB Garamond fonts and wraps the entire app in the global auth and profile providers, while the root page simply redirects to /assistant. The (pages) layout is the authenticated app shell — it guards routes, provides the chat-history and sidebar contexts, and renders the collapsible AppSidebar that links to the assistant, projects, tabular reviews, and workflow library. Those four destinations map one-to-one onto the backend routers from Step 3.
tour.languageLesson: In the Next.js App Router, a folder in parentheses like (pages) is a route group: it lets a set of routes share a layout (here, the authenticated shell) without adding a segment to the URL. Layouts nest, so every page gets the root providers plus the group's auth guard.

tour.title: Session and State Contexts
tour.description: Three React contexts carry the client-side state the shell from Step 9 provides. AuthContext tracks the signed-in Supabase user via a session fetch and auth-state listener — at 23 importers it is the backbone of the authenticated UI; UserProfileContext loads display name, credit usage, tier, and per-provider API-key state from the backend; ChatHistoryContext manages the paginated chat list with optimistic updates. All of them lean on the shared Supabase browser client, whose session token becomes the bearer token that Step 4's middleware validates.

tour.title: Shared Types and API Client
tour.description: These are the two most imported files in the entire codebase. types.ts (53 importers) is the frontend's shared vocabulary: projects, documents, chats, streamed assistant events, edit annotations, citations, tabular reviews, and workflows — the client-side mirror of the database schema from Step 8. mikeApi.ts (37 importers) is the API client that wraps every backend route from Step 3, attaching the Supabase auth token to each request and handling SSE streaming for chats, while modelAvailability maps model ids to providers and gates models behind saved API keys. Master these two files and you can read almost any component in the app.
tour.languageLesson: The streamed assistant events in types.ts are a TypeScript discriminated union: each event shape shares a literal tag field, so a switch on that tag narrows the type and the compiler guarantees every event kind is handled — ideal for SSE protocols with many message types.

tour.title: The Assistant Chat Experience
tour.description: Now the flagship feature end to end. The chat route page loads a conversation by id (or seeds it from a just-started chat handed off via Step 10's context) and renders ChatView wired to useAssistantChat — the core hook that consumes the SSE stream produced by Step 7's engine, drip-feeding content for smooth typing. ChatView renders the message list with citation, document, and edit side panels, and ChatInput supplies attachments, workflow selection, and the model toggle backed by Step 11's availability checks. This is the full loop: input, backend tool loop, streamed render.
tour.languageLesson: Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a one-way HTTP streaming protocol: the server keeps the response open and writes 'data:' lines as they happen. Wrapping the consuming logic in a custom React hook (useAssistantChat) keeps streaming state, buffering, and cleanup out of the components.

tour.title: Project Workspaces
tour.description: Projects are how lawyers organize a matter, persisted in the projects table from Step 8. ProjectsOverview is the dashboard with search, create, rename, and owner-only guards for shared projects; ProjectPage is the workspace itself, a deliberately monolithic component driving the documents tab (folder tree, drag-and-drop uploads and moves, version history, zip download) plus project-scoped chats and tabular reviews through roughly twenty mikeApi calls. FileDirectory and AddDocumentsModal are the shared pickers that let chats anywhere in the app attach these same documents.

tour.title: Tabular Reviews and Workflows
tour.description: The two power features round out the product. TabularReviewView is the highest fan-out component in the codebase: a spreadsheet where each row is a document and each column an extraction question, streaming LLM-generated cells from Step 3's tabular route, with drag-drop document management and Excel export; TRChatPanel adds a citation-aware chat over the same review. The workflow library and its detail editor make prompts reusable assets — a workflow can launch an assistant chat or spawn an entire tabular review, which is how expertise gets shared across a firm.

tour.title: Configuration and Running It Safely
tour.description: Finally, how the pieces from Steps 1-14 get configured and deployed. The backend env template enumerates every external dependency you have met: Supabase service credentials, R2 storage keys, the three LLM provider keys, the HMAC secret for signed downloads, and the encryption secret for stored user API keys; the frontend template holds the public Supabase keys and the backend URL. nixpacks.toml bakes LibreOffice into the deploy image so Step 5's DOCX conversion works in production, and the safe-local-testing guide plus CONTRIBUTING.md show how to develop against disposable resources and ship small, focused PRs.
